Our results demonstrate the potential of RoSmEEry to serve as a valuable benchmark for the development and evaluation of semantic mapping algorithms, and we hope that this dataset will contribute to the advancement of the field.

Rikudo is a Japanese board game that involves strategic placement of tiles to form closed loops. A recent study aimed to determine whether Rikudo could be solved efficiently using a polynomial-time solution, but instead uncovered evidence that Rikudo is in fact a computationally hard problem, with parallels to the well-documented Hamiltonian cycle problem. By mapping the game's state space and applying a reduction technique, researchers were able to demonstrate that Rikudo is in fact a computationally NP-hard problem, with a corresponding time complexity. This finding has significant implications for Rikudo research and will inform the design of future algorithms.

The optimal transport problem is a fundamental concept in mathematics, initially used to determine the distribution of population in demographic studies.  It has since been applied to a wide range of fields including machine learning, computer vision, and physics, where it is used to align two probability distributions by minimizing the cost of transforming one into the other.  The cost of transforming one distribution into another is calculated based on a given cost function, and the optimal transport problem is equivalent to solving a linear programming problem that involves finding the optimal marginal distributions.  In this paper, we investigate the computational complexity of solving the optimal transport problem and present a new algorithm that can efficiently solve large-scale optimal transport problems.  Our approach involves reformulating the linear programming problem as a semidefinite programming problem that can be solved more efficiently.  We also present a new algorithm for solving the optimal transport problem that involves solving the semidefinite programming problem.  Our algorithm is based on a new method for solving the semidefinite programming problem that involves solving the dual problem using a new algorithm.  The new algorithm is an accelerated gradient descent algorithm that can solve the dual problem more efficiently than other existing algorithms.  We also present a new method for solving the primal problem that involves solving the dual problem.  Our algorithm is an accelerated gradient descent algorithm that can solve the primal problem more efficiently than other existing algorithms.  We also present a new method for solving the dual problem that involves solving the dual problem using an accelerated gradient descent algorithm.

This paper provides a comprehensive overview of Ramanujan's work on modular forms and their relationships with Hecke groups. The research includes a proof of Ramanujan's conjecture regarding the sum of squares of Euler's totient function for prime numbers, as well as an exploration of some of the underlying concepts. The paper concludes by highlighting areas where further research is needed in this field.

We have obtained high-resolution spectra of eight lensed quasars using the Keck telescope, each with a different redshift and a range of lensing galaxy redshifts. Our analysis of these spectra has allowed us to determine the redshifts of seven lensing galaxies, with a precision of up to 50 km/s, and the velocity variation of six of these galaxies. The velocity variation of one of these galaxies has been measured for the first time, and the results of our analysis are consistent with previous studies. Our findings will be used to improve the understanding of the evolution of dark energy, and the results of our analysis are expected to contribute to the improvement of the dark energy figure of merit by around 10%.

This research develops a distinct approach for resolving the $q$-fractional differential equation on time scales, and its efficacy is confirmed by several illustrative examples. The findings are supported by theorems and a conclusion, while internal consistency is ensured by logical arguments.

The phonon Hall effect, a phenomenon where sound waves exhibit a quantum spin
Hall effect, has been observed in certain materials. This effect is characterized
by the presence of massless pseudoscalar acoustic modes, which are topological
insulators with a specific edge state. This edge state is a result of the
topological properties of the phonon modes, and its presence has been confirmed
in both theoretical and experimental studies. This effect is a result of the
quantization of the Berry curvature in momentum space, and its presence has
been linked to the presence of Dirac cones in the phonon dispersion relation.
This topological property of the phonon modes is a result of the symmetry of the
material, and it has been observed in certain materials, including graphene and
graphane.

Raman signal sensitivity is significantly enhanced by the technique of Shifted Excitation Raman Difference Spectroscopy (SERDS), which measures the difference in Raman signals generated under two distinct excitation wavelengths. The traditional method of acquiring Raman spectra involves collecting data at two separate excitation energies, which can be time-consuming and may lead to variations in signal quality. To address this limitation, researchers have developed an improved version of SERDS that leverages the Nod and Shuffle Raman technology to accelerate the measurement process. By employing the Nod and Shuffle Raman approach, the technique enables the collection of high-quality Raman spectra at multiple excitation energies in a shorter timeframe, resulting in improved signal-to-noise ratios and enhanced spectral resolution. The effectiveness of the advanced SERDS method is demonstrated through its successful application in various chemical and biological analyses, including the identification of chemical mixtures, the analysis of biological tissues, and the examination of cellular structures.

This paper introduces matrix-based variations of Fejér and Levin-Ste\v{c}kin inequalities for the Moebius transform of a bounded self-adjoint positive operator on a complex Hilbert space. We also derive a matrix-based version of Riemann's localization technique.

We investigate the mean null energy condition for both static and dynamic black holes, employing a holographic framework to model the black hole's thermal radiation. Our analysis reveals that, in the case of static black holes, the mean null energy condition is violated outside the horizon, whereas for dynamic black holes, this condition remains intact outside the horizon, with no effect from thermal radiation.

In the context of conformal field theory, dimensions are fundamental characteristics of primary fields that dictate their behavior. This chapter aims to provide a comprehensive overview of dimensions in conformal field theory, covering both free-field theories and models that interact significantly. It will cover various methods for calculating dimensions, including the algebraic method and algebraic Bethe ansatz, as well as the application of conformal field theory in planar magnetism.

This paper introduces the ICS-CTM2 model, a Cybersecurity Testing Maturity Model for evaluating the reliability of industrial control systems' security. The model assesses the robustness of ICS security control systems through a set of testing criteria, providing a framework to measure an organization's capability to design, execute, and assess the effectiveness of cybersecurity tests. By doing so, the ICS-CTM2 model facilitates the identification of areas for improvement and serves as a standard for organizations to measure their progress in implementing testing methodologies.

In multi-agent reinforcement learning, coordinating the most efficient behavior is a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce a new approach called Greedy-based Worth representation, which assigns a value to each action based on its past performance. This method is then used in a decentralized learning framework, where agents can exchange information and achieve optimal coordination. Experimental results on a complex cooperative problem show that our method performs better than existing approaches.

Pretrained language models have been found to perpetuate various biases, but existing bias assessment tools primarily focus on a single bias type, neglecting the potential for stereotypical bias. This research introduces StereoSet, a novel dataset designed to evaluate stereotypical bias in pretraining corpora. We examine how pretrained models, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, utilize gender-based stereotypes in the long-tail of their corpora. Furthermore, we investigate the effectiveness of bias mitigation techniques, namely prompt calibration and prompt filtering, in reducing stereotypical bias.

The optimization of electrical tilt in offshore wind turbines is a complex task that involves off-shore conditions, turbine design, and blade characteristics. Existing methods for optimizing tilt rely on a cost function that is often derived from onshore testing data, which may not be representative of the off-shore environment. This paper presents an off-policy reinforcement learning approach to develop an optimal electrical tilt policy based on real-world operation data. The method involves creating a tilt policy that maximizes power output based on historical actions and rewards. The approach was tested on a dataset of 25 turbines with 10-year operation history and compared to a baseline model. The results show that the off-policy method outperformed the baseline by 0.8% and 0.4% in terms of power output and efficiency respectively.

A comprehensive assessment of the CKM angle gamma is provided, integrating data from various sources including $B^0 \to \pi^+\pi^-$ and $B^0 \to K^+\K^-$ decays. Furthermore, the analysis involves $B^- \to K^- \pi^+\pi^-$ decays, utilizing data from 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ LHCb dataset. The findings indicate a value of gamma equal to $(103 \pm 42)^\circ$, with the given uncertainty a result of statistical and systematic analysis.

This article explores the geometric properties of an ellipsoid in a three-dimensional space with three distinct complex variables. We establish that the real ellipsoids within this context are connected to specific quadratic equations and provide a method for constructing these ellipsoids based on their defining coefficients. Additionally, we outline a criterion for identifying whether an ellipsoid exhibits rotational symmetry, and finally, we discuss how these complex ellipsoids relate to the geometric structures formed by ellipsoids in a two-dimensional complex plane.

A recent study on personal data trading in the United States found that participants value their data at $1.20 per item. A follow-up study aimed to explore how individuals react to varying prices of data exchanges. The research discovered that individuals tend to become more cautious when data exchanges have higher prices, especially when the unit price exceeds $10. However, it was also observed that individuals are willing to sell their data to multiple buyers, indicating that data sellers are influenced by competition but not necessarily by the number of buyers alone.

In the context of non-orthogonal signaling, we investigate the detection of quicker-than-Nyquist (FTN) constellations, where a continuous-time modulation scheme. To address this, we develop a deep learning-based list sphere decoding (DL-LSD) framework that aims to achieve reliable detection with minimal error rates. The proposed DL-LSD framework is comprised of two stages: a pre-processing stage that utilizes a deep neural network to refine the received signal, and a main processing stage that leverages a convolutional neural network to determine the correct codeword. The proposed DL-LSD framework is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate its superior performance in terms of bit error rate (BER) compared to existing state-of-the-art detectors.

We establish that for an effect algebra Q equipped with a suitable modification of its order topology, the order topology is equivalent to the Frink ideal topology within Q, provided Q's lattice operations are continuous and meet-free collections are contained in any non-empty open set. Additionally, we demonstrate that the collection of non-empty open sets in Q forms a lattice, with its partial order defined by set inclusion. Furthermore, we show that the join of any finite subset of non-empty open sets is the union of those sets, and the join of all non-empty open sets is the entire space Q. These findings are then applied to various types of continuous effect algebras.

To enhance model generalization and robustness, we introduce SaliencyMix, a data augmentation technique that utilizes saliency maps to identify and swap features between images. SaliencyMix aims to simulate the model's focus on specific details during the test phase, thereby improving the model's ability to prioritize relevant features. By combining this approach with existing data augmentation methods, SaliencyMix provides a more effective form of regularization. Experimental results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K datasets demonstrate that SaliencyMix leads to significant improvements in accuracy, with an average boost of 2.5% in validation accuracy across all three datasets.

We investigate the infinite-dimensional Hecke algebra H(Γ) associated with the infinite graph of a regular tree, and focus on its maximal subalgebra, the Iwahori--Hecke algebra H(Γ) (or H(Γ)), which is characterized by a specific set of generators. We introduce a particular basis for H(Γ) and define a natural, non-degenerate pairing that enables the algebra to be embedded within the endomorphism algebra of a vector space. This enables the algebra to be viewed as a general linear algebra over a field, and we proceed to discuss the algebraic and combinatorial properties of H(Γ). We also explore the concept of traces on H(Γ) and demonstrate that the algebraic and combinatorial properties of its traces are equivalent.

Galaxies' intrinsic alignment (IA) can be utilized as a valuable tool for distinguishing between gravitational theories, particularly when their predictions on the correlation between galaxy shapes are compared. A model that accurately describes the correlation between galaxy shapes based on observations suggests that the correlation is largely driven by gravitational forces. However, this model may not be sufficient to capture the full complexity of the correlation between galaxy shapes. In this study, we investigate the correlation between galaxy shapes using a more advanced model that takes into account the alignment of galaxies and their orientation. We then compare the correlation between galaxy shapes with and without the alignment of galaxies, and find that the correlation between galaxy shapes without alignment is significantly weaker than that with alignment. We also find that the correlation between galaxy shapes with and without the alignment of galaxies is largely driven by gravitational forces. Furthermore, we find that the correlation between galaxy shapes with and without the alignment of galaxies can be used to distinguish between gravitational theories, particularly when their predictions on the correlation between galaxy shapes with and without the alignment of galaxies are compared.

In the field of soft matter, the study of deformed particles is gaining significant attention due to their unique properties.  Using computational models, we investigated the behavior of soft particles in a state of fluidity and found that their softness has a profound impact on the way they move and respond to stress.  Our findings revealed that soft particles exhibit distinct patterns of flow and stress that are unlike traditional fluids, and we were able to explain these observations through the particles' ability to change their shape in response to external forces.  Our research has significant implications for understanding the behavior of soft biological materials, and it may also inspire the development of new materials with tailored properties.

The widespread use of gold nanoparticles in various applications is due in part to their unique optical properties, which arise from the localized surface plasmon resonance. However, this phenomenon is highly sensitive to the structural integrity of these nanoparticles, and as such, their melting behavior has garnered significant attention. By combining molecular dynamics simulations with density functional theory, researchers have been able to study the melting behavior of these nanoparticles, and their work has been instrumental in validating experimental results. The authors of this study have taken it a step further by incorporating temperature-dependent density functional theory into their simulations, and their analysis reveals that the melting behavior of these nanoparticles is influenced by the size of the nanoparticle and its surrounding environment. The authors have also developed a new method for characterising the melting behavior of these nanoparticles, and their results show that the nanoparticle's melting behavior is consistent with the Gibbs-Thomson effect. The authors have also found that the melting behavior of these nanoparticles is consistent with the melting behavior of bulk gold, and their work has also shown that the nanoparticle's melting behavior is consistent with the melting behavior of smaller nanoparticles, and their work has also found that the nanoparticle's melting behavior is consistent with the melting behavior of larger nanoparticles, and their work has also found that the nanoparticle's melting behavior is consistent with the nanoparticle's environment.

This is the initial part of a two-paper series that presents novel applications of specific mathematical theorems related to the splitting of solutions. The subsequent paper will focus on practical implementations in the context of the Schrödinger operator, while the current work establishes a general framework for these theorems. By combining and refining existing theories, we develop a method to analyze the behavior of solutions near the boundaries of distinct functional subspaces. This approach is then applied to the parameterized splitting theorems of Reed and Bolton.

The concept of taste is often considered to be a straightforward task, 
with four distinct flavors - sweet, salty, bitter, and umami - being 
commonly recognized. However, the idea of taste is more intricate than 
just categorizing it as sweet, salty, bitter, and umami. This paper 
presents a taste classification system that is grounded in the principles 
of taste receptors and the way people perceive taste. This system is 
represented by a tetrahedron, with its vertices denoting the extremes of 
different taste types. This system is capable of explaining the taste 
properties of various foods and drinks, and it also offers a framework 
for understanding the taste characteristics of psychoactive substances. 
This paper also discusses the potential of this system in the field of 
psychopharmacology, where it can be used to predict the taste properties 
of new compounds.

We derive an alternative representation for the (h;q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials using a Beta function-based approach, also providing a connection between these polynomials and q-Zeta function-related polynomials. Furthermore, our work yields novel identities for the weighted (h;q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials, which are expressed through q-Daehee polynomials.

In clinical trials, researchers often seek to predict the long-term impact of a treatment on patient outcomes. However, many patients do not survive long enough to exhibit this effect, making it difficult to measure. To address this issue, we propose a new method that uses reinforcement learning to estimate treatment effects on long-term health. By treating patient survival as a sequence of repeated trials, we create a policy-based approach that learns the probability of a patient's survival over time. Our method incorporates a policy that reflects the influence of a treatment, allowing us to estimate the treatment's effect on long-term survival. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and real-world data analysis, comparing it to traditional methods and other machine learning techniques.

In case-control studies, researchers often investigate the association between exposure and disease by comparing it with control groups, but these studies can be influenced by memory bias that affects how participants' past exposures and experiences are recalled. To address this issue, we suggest a method that treats recall as a response to exposure, which allows us to quantify the impact of exposure on recall and adjust for this in our analysis. By doing so, we can minimize the distortion in our estimates caused by memory bias and assess the extent to which our findings are influenced by it.

Generative models can be trained in two main ways: either by reconstructing data points directly or by reconstructing latent codes. The latter approach typically involves optimizing the parameters of a probabilistic encoder-decoder model. However, the exact maximum likelihood training method is hindered by the intractability of a key integral in the encoder's distribution. This issue is overcome by employing reversible layers, which can be inverted analytically. This breakthrough enables the use of exact maximum likelihood training for a range of models, including those with discrete inputs. The results show that this method is competitive with other training techniques, even in scenarios where approximate maximum likelihood is used.

The concept of the "smart city" has gained significant attention in recent years, but the rapid advancement of data-driven technologies poses a significant challenge in effectively processing and analyzing vast amounts of urban data. To address this issue, we present a novel, user-friendly data visualization tool that enables citizens to uncover valuable insights from smart city data. By leveraging correlation analysis, our system identifies connections between various urban attributes, such as traffic congestion, noise pollution, and energy consumption, and presents them in a clear and understandable manner. To facilitate exploration, we have developed a set of interactive visualizations that allow users to navigate and drill down into different data attributes, and ultimately, to gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationships within urban data.

This study introduces a novel geometric multigrid preconditioning method tailored to the HDG-P0 formulation of reaction-diffusion and generalized Stokes equations. By leveraging the HDG-P0 scheme's localized and decoupled system matrix structure, we establish a multigrid preconditioner that optimizes performance. Our method involves a static condensation approach to decouple local HDG variables and a novel coarse space defined by coarse elements' average values. By applying this preconditioner to a uniform coarse mesh and a non-uniform fine mesh, we demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving robust convergence.

In situations where data collection is incomplete, the uncertainty surrounding the findings is often underestimated due to the unquantifiable nature of missing data. This letter presents a Bayesian method to evaluate how missing data sensitivity affects the reliability of inferences. By employing a probabilistic approach, the analysis is based on the expected information value, denoted as the E-value. This metric is calculated from the posterior distribution, allowing for the quantification of the impact of missing data on the likelihood of drawing accurate conclusions. The proposed method is applied to a meta-analysis case study and compared to the traditional frequentist approach, demonstrating its ability to provide more precise estimates of the reliability of inferences.

In crossover trials where subjects are randomly assigned to groups and then undergo distinct sequences of treatments, the design is typically used to minimize bias and maximize statistical power. However, due to the sequential nature of these studies, the occurrence of missing data is a significant concern. To address this issue, the current study proposes a novel approach to handle missing data based on probability. This approach involves analyzing the crossover design using multiple imputation and the multiple imputation estimation method. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the methodology is applied to a real-world clinical trial involving patients with rheumatoid arthritis who were treated with various combinations of methotrexate and a TNF-alpha inhibitor.

We introduce the concept of a $C$-bialgebra within a given monoidal category $C$, and explore its inherent properties. This notion is analogous to traditional bialgebraic structures but is formulated independently of specific categories. Instead, it is derived from the inherent properties of $C$. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the concept of a $C$-bialgebra and the geometric theory of associahedra, specifically through the use of a suitable monoidal category $C$ that is equivalent to a category of geometric shapes.

To improve the performance of specific applications, researchers have introduced in-memory computing (IMC) that integrates processing near the storage location.  However, the performance of IMC is hindered by the limitations of DRAM, which is the most commonly used memory technology.  To address this challenge, we have developed a new approach that allows for the creation of custom in-memory computing systems by modifying existing DRAM chips.  Our approach involves the use of a new tool called CODIC, which enables the implementation of in-memory computing systems at a low cost.  CODIC is based on a new framework that allows for the modification of DRAM chips using a commercial tool called DRAM-Aware Programming (DAP).  Our results show that CODIC can be used to create in-memory computing systems that outperform traditional DRAM by up to 2.5x for certain applications.  Furthermore, the cost of implementing these systems using CODIC is significantly lower than that of using other approaches, with a savings of up to 90%.

This paper is a continuation of our earlier work, in which we utilized functional programming to effectively manage and coordinate virtualized network resources. In this study, we delve into the role of functional programming in facilitating network evolution and design, with a focus on the services it provides. We propose a novel, high-level abstraction called 'networking function' to capture the dynamic nature of networks, and to enable the creation of virtualized networks. To demonstrate the practical application of our approach, we present a real-world example, in which the 'networking function' abstraction is used to design a network for a virtual data center.

In quantum computing, a key objective is to create a universal quantum processor, which can execute any quantum operation. We've developed a universal quantum processor based on a toric code, utilizing a combination of two-qubit and multi-qubit gates. This processor leverages a toric code, where each qubit in a surface code corresponds to a physical qubit in a lattice. We've identified a set of gates that can be implemented using a combination of local operations and two-qubit gates. These gates enable the creation of a universal set, which can be used to perform any quantum operation. We've also demonstrated that our processor can be used to perform any multi-qubit operation with a number of gates proportional to the number of qubits, while maintaining a logarithmic scaling factor.

The OPUS system is a task control system that enables users to manage and 
coordinate the operation of multiple observatory systems through a unified 
interface. Developed by the Australian Observatory, OPUS is built upon 
established VO standards and protocols, making it an interoperable system 
that facilitates communication between the system and various observatory 
systems via standard protocols. As a result, users can access and manage 
observatory resources, including scheduling tasks, via a web-based client, 
while the system also supports direct interaction through command-line tools 
and APIs.

A novel approach to educational learning is presented, which leverages digital game-based learning to educate users about intricate complex wireless networks. This methodology empowers users to construct and manage their own network simulations, thereby fostering a comprehensive understanding of the subject matter. Through interactive gameplay, users can develop and refine their problem-solving skills, thereby gaining a deeper comprehension of the network's functionality. This methodology is exemplified by a case study, which demonstrates its potential to educate users about SDN and 5G networks.

The relationship between ozone and oxygen levels in planetary atmospheres has been studied to understand the composition of atmospheres that are similar to Earth's. Using a 1D radiative transfer model, we simulated various atmospheric conditions with different temperatures, pressures, and compositions, as well as the presence of aerosols. We found that the ozone formation is highly sensitive to the photon flux, which is influenced by the atmospheric pressure and temperature. We also found that the ozone to oxygen ratio is not constant across different atmospheres, but rather depends on the specific conditions. In particular, we found that the ozone to oxygen ratio is higher in atmospheres with lower temperatures and pressures, but lower in atmospheres with higher temperatures and pressures. We also found that the ozone to oxygen ratio is higher in atmospheres with higher oxygen levels, but lower in atmospheres with lower oxygen levels. These results suggest that the ozone to oxygen ratio is not a reliable indicator of oxygen levels in planetary atmospheres, but rather depends on the specific conditions.

We investigate the behavior of nonequilibrium physics in a three-dimensional lattice model with a topological structure, where an electric field is applied in a two-dimensional section. This leads to the emergence of directed currents on the surface, influenced by the magnetic flux passing through the three-dimensional volume. The resulting electric field is a stable, non-equilibrium phenomenon, resistant to changes in the number of particles and their distribution, and can be modified by adjusting the potential energy on the surface. The unique topological structure of the model allows for the presence of directed currents with a topological invariant that is not affected by the surface's properties.

Recent advancements in Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (MNMT) have led to significant improvements in translating languages with limited translation resources. However, these models often struggle with translating specialized domains such as medicine, which can result in inaccurate interpretations. To address this issue, we present a novel approach that leverages the power of domain-specific information from parallel corpora in MNMT. Our proposed method, Domain-Adapted Multilingual Neural Machine Interpretation (DAMINI), utilizes a two-stage adaptation process to fine-tune the model for medical translation. The first stage involves training the model on a small, specialized dataset, while the second stage refines it using a larger, general medical dataset. Our experimental results demonstrate that DAMINI outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both automatic and visual evaluation metrics.

A theoretical investigation into the properties of altered-ion-acoustic waves in a plasma system containing electrons, ions, and positively charged dust particles has been conducted. The study considered a two-temperature electron population and employed the reductive perturbation method to derive nonlinear equations describing solitary and shock waves. The findings revealed that the speed of these waves is influenced by the density of both ion and dust particles, as well as the temperature of ion fluid and the number of positive charges carried by dust particles. The results also indicated that the compressive nature of these waves can be altered by adjusting the density of positively charged dust particles. Furthermore, the study showed that the existence of a solitary wave depends on the density of positively charged dust particles, while the shock wave's speed was found to be dependent on the number of positive charges carried by dust particles.

This study introduces an unsupervised approach to pre-training sentence representations across multiple languages, focusing on enhancing retrieval efficiency in cross-lingual settings. Our method, which incorporates contextual awareness, enables the development of pre-trained models that can be effectively fine-tuned for ranking tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by creating a pre-trained model that achieves state-of-the-art results in compact cross-lingual sentence representation retrieval, outperforming a leading model across five evaluation languages and 11 language pairs.

Multimodal learning models often rely on a straightforward approach, combining separate unimodal representations to form a comprehensive one. However, this approach overlooks the possibility that different modalities may have distinct perspectives on the same concept. This insight motivates the development of a novel multimodal model that allows for the adjustment of individual modalities in relation to a shared concept. By doing so, the model can better distinguish between the inherent and extraneous information within each modality. We introduce a new method, prototypical modal adjustment (PMR), which enables the refinement of unimodal representations by subtracting the shared concept's extraneous information. This process is facilitated by a prototypical contrastive learning framework that simultaneously learns concept representations and their extraneous counterparts. This approach is versatile and can be applied to various multimodal tasks, including classification and retrieval. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing methods in both scenarios.

In the context of heavy-ion collisions, we develop a transport theory model that incorporates vector mesons into Quark-Gluon Plasma dynamics. By utilizing the Dyson-Schwinger equation, we establish non-perturbative models for various hadron scattering cross sections, taking into account the effects of strong correlations among quarks and non-quark particles. The interaction of quarks with vector mesons is also considered, leading to the emergence of hadron resonances through coupled-channel scattering. Our model predicts the formation of hadronic gas composed of stable hadrons and resonances, which can be compared to experimental data.

This study introduces a novel approach to spoken command recognition, which combines a deep neural network with a tensor-train network. The proposed hybrid model leverages the strengths of both, utilizing a pre-trained convolutional neural network to generate feature maps that are then compressed using a fully connected tensor-train network. The resulting model is then optimized using a two-stream architecture, which is evaluated on the Alexa-Command and Alexa-Toy-Box datasets. The experiments demonstrate that the proposed hybrid model outperforms a traditional CNN in spoken command recognition, with significant improvements in both micro- and macro-averaged F1 scores.

We illustrate the process of deriving non-Markovian quantum dynamics for a system in contact with a harmonic environment by using various master equation forms. Specifically, we demonstrate how to obtain a stochastic Schrödinger equation from both a non-Markovian quantum master equation and a time-local quantum master equation under specific assumptions. The two approaches are shown to yield identical non-Markovian quantum dynamics for the system, which can be further analyzed using the quantum-jump formalism.

This study explores the effects of varying the shape of aluminum nanoparticles on the efficiency of silicon thin-film solar panels. By analyzing the optical absorption within these panels through simulations, we discovered that nanoparticles with a specific ellipsoidal shape lead to the greatest absorption enhancement. Our findings also reveal that increasing the size of these ellipsoidal nanoparticles results in a significant rise in absorption, with the optimal size found to be around 100 nanometers. Notably, our research indicates that the spherical shape previously used in these applications is suboptimal, with the elliptical shape offering a 10% improvement in absorption.

We investigate the capacity of a first-order logic system, denoted as FO$\mathcal{E}^*$, that incorporates a choice operator but excludes enumeration, and is grounded in the polynomial time logic framework. FO$\mathcal{E}^*$ is distinguished by its inclusion of a construct that facilitates the creation of finite sets and its inability to access the values of variables in these sets. Our research demonstrates that FO$\mathcal{E}^*$ is capable of expressing the solutions to certain problems within the realm of constraint satisfaction problems, including the assessment of the sizes of these sets. Furthermore, we establish that FO$\mathcal{E}^*$ is not capable of expressing the solutions to certain problems within the realm of counting problems, including the assessment of the sizes of these sets.

Deep learning models, particularly those based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have been successfully applied to video recognition tasks. However, their large size poses significant challenges for implementation on resource-constrained devices. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that integrates Algorithm-Hardware co-design to create energy-efficient LSTM networks. By utilizing Hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition, we can break down large weight matrices into a more compact, sparse form, reducing memory requirements and computational costs. The decomposed model can be efficiently executed on a custom hardware accelerator, where the computation is distributed across a cluster of processing elements. The processing elements are connected by a hierarchical interconnect, allowing for parallel computation. The proposed approach has been evaluated on a video recognition task, where the Hierarchical Tucker decomposition outperforms other tensor-based methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The resulting hardware accelerator has been implemented on an Intel Stratix V FPGA, demonstrating a significant reduction in energy consumption and acceleration of computation, with a notable improvement of 3.5 times the baseline frequency.

The MAVLink protocol, widely used in unmanned systems, is susceptible to attacks due to its outdated design. These vulnerabilities can compromise the security of critical systems such as Ardupilot and PX4, making them vulnerable to attacks. Our research focuses on MAVLink's security weaknesses and develops a security framework to protect it. This framework includes a secure proxy capable of detecting and preventing malicious commands, as well as a system for authenticating commands and detecting potential threats. Our findings were tested on a real-world drone and demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed solution in preventing attacks.

A network simulator called Kollaps, designed for Linux and commodity hardware, emulates various network conditions, including congestion, packet loss, and delay. This emulator operates in a distributed manner, replicating real-world topologies based on the structure of the Internet. Kollaps utilizes the Netfilter framework to introduce random fluctuations in the simulated network behavior, specifically the congestion windows of TCP connections. This feature allows for the creation of diverse network conditions, including varying packet loss rates and network dynamics, without the need for centralized control. Kollaps is capable of simulating complex network behaviors, including congestion collapse and packet bursting, and can be applied to a wide range of network simulations, including those involving multiple TCP connections.

The Newman-Penrose map's connection to twistor space roots explored, particularly in relation to its boundary limits. The extent to which these roots represent complete twistor space projections is investigated alongside an examination of potential limitations.

The Muon Surface Detector, a cutting-edge, underground detector, utilizes
muons to study the Earth's subsurface composition. This detector is a key
component of the DUNE far detector, designed to detect long-baseline
neutrino anomalies. The Muon SD leverages charge-sensitive silicon detectors
to identify and count muons, with each unit consisting of a silicon detector
and a readout system. The detector's performance, including its ability to
accurately locate muons, will be demonstrated through laboratory tests and
cosmic-ray measurements.

This technical report introduces a formal specification for Parsing Expression Language, a concise parsing tool that builds upon Regular Expressions. The framework is formally established within the framework of Expressive Languages with Parsing Expression Grammar, allowing for a clear definition of the Parsing Expression Language. Furthermore, we outline the structural framework of PEL, its key components, and the underlying parsing process. Additionally, this report presents a concise summary of the standard semantics of PEL, as well as an annotated grammar for LLP, the Language of Linguistic Parsing, which serves as an extension of PEL.

In this research, we investigate how a $U(1)$ gauge theory in a $d$-dimensional spacetime, under conditions of high temperature and non-zero electric field, leads to the emission of Cherenkov radiation. The study involves calculating the energy loss of charged particles through this process, and determining the emission spectrum. The findings suggest that as temperature increases, the emission rate of this process will also rise. The results obtained can be applied to a variety of real-world contexts, including the study of particle acceleration in laboratory settings and the emission of radiation in certain types of cosmic string defects.

To study how language evolves with time, researchers have been analyzing
language trends over the past few decades, but there's a significant gap in
our understanding of predictions about language futures. To address this,
we've developed a new method that uses neural language models to track
forecasts of linguistic changes. By applying this method to forecasts made
by humans and to the predictions of neural models, we've found that these
models can accurately replicate human forecasts of future language trends.
Furthermore, we've discovered that fine-tuning these models on human data
improves their ability to predict future language trends.

We introduce a straightforward yet powerful technique for estimating the three-dimensional pose of a given object from a single image, relying solely on a single image without the need for a pre-existing 3D model. This approach leverages the observation that when an object is rotated, its surface features create shading effects, providing crucial information about its underlying geometry. By analyzing these shading effects, we can derive constraints on the object's surface geometry, enabling us to accurately determine its three-dimensional pose. To achieve this, we develop a novel image synthesis method that generates a set of candidate poses, each corresponding to a specific object rotation. We then employ a neural network to predict the shading effects resulting from these rotations, using a loss function that penalizes the network for discrepancies between its predictions and actual shading effects. This approach is highly versatile, requiring only a single image to accurately determine the object's three-dimensional pose. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a range of challenging real-world datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods in all cases.

We have investigated the phenomenon of controlled crossed Andreev tunneling and elastic co-reflection in a hybrid structure comprising two semiconductor quantum wells, a superconductor, and a metal gate. The superconductor and metal gate are positioned between the quantum wells to facilitate the transfer of quasiparticles between them. The superconductor and metal gate also act as electrodes to induce Andreev bound states in the semiconductor, which can be manipulated by adjusting the voltage applied to the metal gate. Our findings indicate that the hybrid structure can be used to control the transport of quasiparticles, with the potential to develop a novel device capable of manipulating spin-orbit interactions and Andreev bound states.

To investigate the impact of an anisotropic velocity distribution on particle acceleration during magnetic reconnection, a 2D simulation model was developed. This model incorporated a velocity distribution with a specified scattering angle, allowing for the simulation of anisotropic conditions. The simulation found that anisotropic conditions significantly enhance the acceleration of particles, with a velocity distribution's specified scattering angle playing a key role. Particles with higher energies exhibit a greater scattering angle, and their energy distribution follows a power-law pattern with a steep index. The simulation results also show that anisotropic conditions lead to a greater conversion of magnetic energy into kinetic energy, and a more efficient production of high-energy particles.

We investigate the feasibility of discovering new physics through the measurement of the Higgs boson width in $e^+e^-\to Zh$ and Higgs diphoton decay rates at future $e^+e^-$ colliders. Our analysis is conducted within the framework of the Standard Model extended by a complex triplet scalar field, which is a common basis for various extensions of the Standard Model. The results show that the Higgs boson width measurement in $e^++e^-\to Zh$ can be highly sensitive to the parameters of the triplet scalar field, especially when the triplet scalar is light. Furthermore, we find that the Higgs diphoton rate can be significantly affected by the triplet scalar field, especially when the triplet scalar is heavy. Our findings suggest that the Higgs diphoton rate can be used to probe the triplet scalar field, especially when the triplet scalar is heavy.

The numerical radius of a bounded linear operator in a complex Hilbert space is a normed function that measures its average behavior between input and output spaces. The combined numerical radius, introduced in 2016, is a more comprehensive form of the numerical radius, taking into account the minimum of two possible values, both related to the range and intersection of the operator's input and output spaces. In this work, we investigate the subdifferential of this combined numerical radius, demonstrating that it exists and can be calculated in terms of the minimum eigenvalues of the operator's adjoint and a specific matrix related to the range of the operator. This finding has potential applications in the study of operator matrices and allows us to derive inequalities related to the minimum eigenvalue of the operator.

The growing interest in data privacy has led to a surge in research focused on protecting sensitive information. This study examines the potential applications of differential privacy in safeguarding financial data, highlighting its benefits and key takeaways. By applying the principles of differential privacy, financial institutions can develop innovative solutions to address pressing issues like data breaches, data anonymization, and machine learning. This work aims to inspire the development of new financial applications that utilize differential privacy to ensure data security and protect user privacy.

This research paper explores the concept of a stochastic mapping, which is a mapping between two random spaces, and examines its properties, particularly how it relates to the correlation between input and output random fields. The paper demonstrates that stochastic mapping can be viewed as a specific type of random dispersion matrix and proves that the mapping's kernel is directly related to the Green's function of the Fokker-Planck equation. The paper also introduces a new class of stochastic mappings with a stationary correlation function, which can be applied to study the behavior of random dispersion fields in various media, such as porous materials and random composite materials. The paper's findings are illustrated with numerical examples, which show the impact of different types of stochastic mappings on the behavior of random dispersion fields.

The potential for high-pressure hydrogen fuel in future energy systems is substantial, but ensuring its safe transportation and storage is a pressing concern.  A novel method for detecting hydrogen has been developed using a high-pressure mixture of He, H2, and O2, ignited by an undirected laser beam.  This method is based on a shock-driven self-igniting process, which was modeled using a combination of the Euler equations and a reactive model.  A key finding is that the undirected laser beam can induce a shock wave in the hydrogen mixture, which can then ignite and propagate rapidly.  This process can be controlled by adjusting the laser energy and the mixture composition, and can be used to detect hydrogen in a variety of conditions.  This method offers a promising approach to detecting hydrogen safely and efficiently at high pressures.

Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved semantic segmentation tasks. However, existing models often struggle with accurately predicting boundaries due to the lack of boundary information. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel boundary-aware segmentation network that generates boundary maps, which are then combined with predicted pixel labels to refine segmentation results. Our approach is particularly beneficial for mobile and web applications, where pixel-level boundaries are often difficult to define. To enhance the model's generalizability, we incorporate a domain adaptation module that enables the network to adapt to new domains with limited labeled data. We evaluate our method on multiple datasets and observe substantial improvements in boundary prediction and segmentation results. Notably, our model achieves a high accuracy of 90.5% in predicting boundaries, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods.

This research introduces a groundbreaking driver messenger system, which utilizes vehicle-to-vehicle communication to convey driver intentions via natural language. The system aims to enhance lane change processes by allowing drivers to negotiate using messages, with the goal of reducing accidents caused by miscommunication. A prototype was developed, and its components - including a natural language processing system, text-to-speech functionality, and message exchange via DSMS - were tested in a real-world setting, with the system being evaluated through user studies.

The movement of non-interacting, weakly active particles within confined spaces is studied. In the context of the active Brownian suspension model, the particles' behavior is described by a stochastic Liouville equation, solved using a finite element method. To explore the impact of various confining shapes on the particles' stationary distribution, different geometries are examined. Notably, the presence of a soft boundary is found to significantly affect the stationary distribution, as it alters the direction of the drift velocity. A comparative analysis is conducted to evaluate the effects of soft and no-flow boundary conditions.

The average particle number operator has a distinct set of eigenstates known as Siegert states that are associated with the eigenvalues representing particle number. These states are separate from the primary ground state and the excited states found within the traditional Fock space. Research has shown that the Siegert states play a significant role in the decay processes of unstable nuclei, particularly in the decay of alpha particles. In this context, the average particle number operator is examined, and the resulting eigenstates are found to be a combination of Fock states. This discovery reveals that the average particle number operator has a limited set of eigenstates, with the remaining states being non-hermitian and referred to as Siegert states.

Observations of the Si IV 1398 Angstrom line in a solar flare captured by the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph revealed rapid changes in the line's intensity and profiles, which occurred within a 10-40 second time frame. These changes were localized to a 10 arc-second region surrounding the X-ray flare peak and showed a distinct pattern of initial cooling followed by heating. The line's intensity variations were found to be closely linked to the changes in the electron temperature and density, and the line's Doppler width exhibited a rapid increase during this period. These observations suggest that the observed changes were due to the rapid expansion of high-temperature plasma, which was likely the result of magnetic reconnection.

The strong CP problem, tied to the axion, has garnered significant attention.  However, the axion's ultimate fate, whether it will be a light or heavy particle, remains uncertain.  This article will examine the strong CP problem, the axion, and related research findings, focusing on the axion's potential implications for low-energy physics and high-energy matter.

The critical angle of total external refraction for light traveling from a medium with a lower to one with a higher refractive index is a useful indicator for identifying nanostructured patterns within thin films. Researchers have discovered that this approach can be used to detect irradiation-induced nanostructured patterns within thin films without relying on prior knowledge of the pattern's morphology. A comprehensive model has been developed to calculate the critical angle of total external refraction, taking into account the patterned morphology within irradiated thin films. This model utilizes a probabilistic framework to determine the spatial distribution of ion-induced damage, which is then used to calculate the critical angle. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to various thin film systems, including silicon dioxide and silicon nitride, irradiated with ions of varying energies. The results show that the critical angle of total external refraction can be used to detect nanostructured patterns within thin films, regardless of whether they are columnar or amorphous in nature.

Plagiarism detection in source code is a complex issue, and existing methods have their limitations. While traditional plagiarism metrics are effective for detecting the extent of plagiarism, they fail to identify the underlying intent. On the other hand, intent-based approaches are not suitable for large-scale applications due to their high computational requirements. This paper presents an innovative solution to bridge this gap, and demonstrates its feasibility by translating the proposed algorithm into a C# program.

The article examines the convergence properties of specific Dirichlet series, which are defined by particular types of Dirichlet characters satisfying a Weyl sum condition, and related to the Riemann zeta function. This investigation builds on the research of Chambert-Loir and Pollicott, and involves a comparison with the results of Baker and Chinwala, and of Bourgain, Gambhir, Hilberdink, and Miller.

We establish that in metric spaces, near semigroups and near groups can be defined using specific epsilon values. Specifically, for any semigroup S and given epsilon greater than 0, a subgroup G of S can be found such that the distance between G raised to the power of any s in S and G is less than epsilon. Furthermore, for any group G and given epsilon greater than 0, a semigroup H can be found such that the distance between G and H is less than epsilon. Additionally, for any subgroup G of a semigroup S and given epsilon greater than 0, a subgroup G' can be found such that the distance between G and G' is less than epsilon and G' is a subset of S.

We introduce a novel computational system for estimating densities in high dimensions, specifically for log-concave distributions. Our approach diverges from traditional methods based on Bayesian inference and instead relies on a primal-dual optimization technique to efficiently select the best bandwidth factors. This allows for rapid and scalable density estimation, with computational costs increasing linearly with the number of variables. Our implementation in the logcon concentration package for R outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and reliability, with further details and implementation specifics available on the author's website.

A novel approach is introduced to efficiently sample the vast configuration space of static granular packs, focusing on the volume occupation of individual particles. The proposed method relies on the Wang-Landau algorithm, which assigns a uniform entropy to distinct volume configurations, disregarding the particles' spatial arrangement. This entropy-based approach is more efficient than traditional Monte Carlo sampling methods, as it prioritizes the volume configuration rather than the particle arrangement. The proposed method is particularly effective in analyzing the statistical properties of granular packs, such as the radial distribution function, even when the particles' arrangement is highly disordered. The method's applicability is not limited to granular packs, but can be extended to any system with well-defined volume occupation.

The adventurer and security director in a graph-based game engage in a zero-sum competition. The security director is aware of the graph's structure and can place cameras on vertices to monitor the adventurer's movements. The adventurer, however, only sees distances between vertices. Their objective is for the adventurer to reach a target vertex while the director slows them down. This scenario is analyzed in relation to the graph's spectral properties, spectral radius, and longest path. The game's complexity is also examined in terms of the adventurer's information advantage and the limit of the game's duration approaching infinity.

The spectral density of a stochastic process is a key indicator of its temporal behavior, but its relationship with the process itself is not well understood, particularly in terms of how frequencies are connected. We investigate this connection for Gaussian processes by analyzing the autocorrelation function and its relationship with the spectral density. We find that the autocorrelation function can be represented as a Fourier transform of the spectral density, and certain properties of the spectral density can be inferred from the autocorrelation function. We then use these findings to propose a model of single-trajectory spectral density, which is a key component in certain statistical analyses of time series data. We validate our model through numerical simulations and demonstrate its relationship with the autocorrelation function.

This study focuses on the (1+1)-dimensional Broer-Kaup system, a model that incorporates higher-order nonlinearities, and investigates its soliton solutions through the interaction of two solitary waves. By employing the Kaup-Newell reduction method, we derive a pair of solitary waves from the system's singular solitary wave solutions. Subsequently, we analyze the soliton interaction within the (1+1)-dimensional Broer-Kaup system, utilizing the derived solitary wave solutions, and provide a detailed analysis of the soliton's shape deformation during the interaction process.

This study focuses on preserving energy in weak solutions to the incompressible Euler equations through vorticity. We establish that weak solutions with positive vorticity and initial energy exceeding a specified value will conserve energy. The proof involves two key steps: first, proving the existence of weak solutions with positive vorticity, and second, demonstrating that these solutions conserve their initial energy. The existence of these solutions is established by adapting the approach of Wu-Yu in 2017, while the conservation of energy is proven by building upon the work of Chen-Lin in 2020, who initially showed that weak solutions with positive vorticity and additional properties conserve their energy.

The VIRUP project offers an immersive experience, allowing users to step into a virtual world that simulates a universe with a unique, hypothetical set of properties.  This simulated world is based on an innovative mathematical concept that redefines the fundamental relationship between energy and time.  By contrast to the real universe, in the VIRUP universe, energy is time's primary determinant, and time is a function of energy.  This virtual world's underlying physics is grounded in a new equation that reconciles two fundamental principles: the conservation of energy and the change over time.  This equation, a variation of the Hamiltonian equation, is derived from the principles of quantum mechanics and applied to the entire universe, rather than isolated systems.  As a result, the VIRUP universe is governed by a unique set of physical laws, which are distinct from those of the real universe.  This virtual world is accessible through a software platform, allowing users to explore and experience its properties.

A hands-on, interactive approach is missing from the way data is currently presented, which can make it difficult for the general public to understand. To address this issue, we developed a user-friendly data visualization tool called Space Voyage, designed specifically for kids as young as 9 to 14 years old. This tool enables them to collect data on their physical characteristics, track their progress over time, and make informed comparisons with their peers. Through the use of Data Bricks, a platform that facilitates seamless data analysis, our young participants discovered first-hand how data can be transformed into meaningful information. The positive feedback from our pilot study indicates that Space Voyage effectively engages kids in data-related activities and fosters their interest in data literacy.

In software defined networking, traffic patterns within the data-plane are analyzed to identify the underlying data flows. This analysis is done by examining the data-plane's operational flows, which are sequences of packets processed by the data-plane's current configuration. However, existing methods for identifying these flows are limited, as they rely on making assumptions about the network's configuration and behavior. To address this issue, we present a new approach that leverages the data-plane's operational data flows, which are sequences of data flows observed in the data-plane. This approach does not require knowledge of the network's configuration and can be applied to any data-plane implementation. We have developed a tool called FlowMiner that can extract and analyze the data-plane's operational data flows, allowing for the identification of the underlying data flows. Our results show that FlowMiner is effective in accurately identifying data flows in real-world scenarios, with an average accuracy rate of 95%.

Recent advancements in disentangled representation learning have focused on utilizing relational information to develop more robust and interpretable features. However, most existing methods rely on strong prior knowledge, which is not always feasible in practical applications. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework that leverages relational information to achieve weakly disentangled representations without requiring such prior knowledge. Our approach is built upon the concept of variational autoencoders and incorporates a novel prior that utilizes relational information to enhance representation learning. To facilitate learning, we propose a contrastive regularizer that encourages the model to represent objects based on their class labels. Our experiments on various datasets demonstrate that this approach effectively leverages relational information to achieve state-of-the-art weakly disentangled representations.

The performance of oscillating foil arrays, which harness energy from ocean waves, is influenced by the interaction between the foil and the complex flow around it. This study uses a numerical model to analyze the impact of the foil's movement on its performance in arrays, with a focus on how the foil's shape changes affect energy production. The research shows that when the foil's movement becomes unstable, its performance is significantly reduced, and that by adjusting the foil's movement, it's possible to increase the amount of energy collected from the ocean waves, with optimal results achieved when both foils move in sync.

We've developed a Bayesian method to calculate the real-time evolution of correlation functions using lattice QCD. This approach allows us to accurately estimate the uncertainty of our results and can be applied to a wide range of observables. We've tested our method by analyzing the time-evolution of a harmonic oscillator's wave function, comparing it to the traditional real-time formalism. We've also applied our method to the anharmonic chain's expectation value of the square of its Hamiltonian, finding that the results are consistent with the harmonic oscillator's behavior. We've demonstrated that our method can be used to constrain the parameters of a model Hamiltonian, and we've shown that it can be used to calculate the real-time evolution of a system's wave function when the initial state is unknown.

We have developed a novel approach to study the interaction between a quantum dot and a superconducting island at low temperatures. By applying a gate voltage, we can switch the quantum dot between being connected and disconnected from the island, effectively toggling the superconducting link on and off. When the quantum dot is disconnected, it absorbs charge from the island, causing the superconductor to transition into the insulating state. In contrast, when it is connected, it donates charge to the island, resulting in the restoration of the superconducting state. By measuring the associated changes in gate voltage, we can accurately determine the amount of charge transferred between the dot and the island, as well as the critical current threshold. Our findings show that the quantum dot's behavior is consistent with the Andreev reflection process, and we have successfully extracted the relevant parameters of this process.

The primary goal of drug discovery is to develop novel compounds with specific therapeutic effects. In this research, we introduce a pioneering approach to generative models, which leverages a unique energy function tailored to a specific target to produce target-specific compounds. Our proposed model, which combines the Dijkstra algorithm with a generative adversarial network, is trained on a dataset of target-specific compounds and a graph of interacting molecular bonds. Upon generation, the compound is evaluated for its efficacy against a target using molecular docking simulations. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach using a dataset of HIV protease inhibitors, which resulted in a significant improvement in target-specificity compared to a generative adversarial network.

The Geometry of Interaction approach to reducing program termination has been widely applied in various programming languages and systems. A key concept in this approach is the token, which represents a program's instruction and serves as a guide for the program's execution. To enhance the efficiency of the Geometry of Interaction method, a new device is proposed that integrates token information into a graph structure. This innovative device is termed the Token-Guided Graph. It is based on a mathematical concept called a hypergraph, which allows for the representation of tokens and their interactions. A hypergraph's edge is used to represent a program's instruction, and its vertex represents the program's data. By using hyperedges to guide the program's execution, the Token-Guided Graph can be transformed into a program counter-guided graph, which is a more efficient and reliable method for reducing program termination. A key benefit of the Token-Guided Graph is its ability to handle complex programs with multiple instructions and data, making it a more versatile and efficient tool for program reduction.

We have conducted a comprehensive study of the Large Magellanic Cloud's (LMC) outer region, utilizing data from the VMC survey. By combining optical and near-infrared data, we were able to identify a distinct population of stars in the LMC's outer region, which we believe to be the result of the SMC's collision with the LMC. Our analysis of proper motion in the LMC's outer region revealed a bimodal pattern, which we attribute to the influence of the SMC. We found that stars in the LMC's outer region exhibit a higher velocity of approximately 60 km/s in the direction of the SMC, which is consistent with the SMC's motion. Our findings suggest that the SMC's collision with the LMC has had a profound impact on the LMC's outer region, which we believe to be the result of the SMC's ram pressure.

The widespread adoption of Advanced Metering Infrastructures (AMI) has enabled utilities to monitor energy consumption in real-time, but also left them vulnerable to cyber-attacks. A particularly damaging attack, known as a power theft attack, can be executed by exploiting vulnerabilities in AMI systems. To counteract this threat, a novel deep learning-based detection framework is proposed, utilizing a combination of recurrent neural networks and convolutional layers to analyze AMI data. The proposed framework's performance is evaluated using a dataset of simulated power theft attacks, and the results demonstrate its ability to accurately identify attacks, even with minimal data. Furthermore, the framework's adaptability is showcased through its ability to be fine-tuned for optimal performance using a variety of hyper-parameter optimization algorithms.

We investigate the properties of compact surfaces equipped with a collection of disjoint, embedded graphs. A key result shows that the surface's fundamental group depends on the topological features of the graphs. Specifically, the graphs' connected components, their cycle structures, and the ways in which they connect to form a network determine the fundamental group. This result has significant implications for understanding the properties of minimal surfaces in physics, particularly those of Wilson loops in quantum gravity models.

The lifetime of the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ baryon has been measured for the first time using data collected by the LHCb detector in proton-proton collisions at energies of 13 TeV, corresponding to data accumulation of 6 inverse femtobarns. This measurement was based on  $p p \to p D^{*+} K^{-}\pi^{+}\pi^{-}$ events, where $D^{*+}$ decays to $D^{0}\pi^{+}\pi^{+}\pi^{-}$, and the $D^{0}$ decayed to $K^{+}K^{-}\pi^{+}\pi^{-}$. The lifetime of the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ baryon was found to be $ 196.9^{+2.2}_{-2.3}^{+1.1}_{-1.0}$ picoseconds. Additionally, the lifetime of the $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryon was measured for the first time using data collected by the LHCb detector in proton-proton collisions at energies of 13 TeV, corresponding to data accumulation of 5 inverse femtobarns. This measurement was based on  $p p \to p D^{*+} K^{-}\pi^{+}\pi^{-}$ events, where $D^{*+}$ decays to $D^{0}\pi^{+}\pi^{+}\pi^{-}$

Unsupervised subspace clustering has been a crucial yet under-researched aspect of hyperspectral image classification. This paper presents a rapid and accurate method for subspace clustering based on similarity constraints, which incorporates a novel, efficient subspace clustering technique and a self-supervised learning approach to optimize the similarity constraints. Initially, the proposed method utilizes a novel, efficient subspace clustering technique to identify similar pixels in the image, which are then grouped into clusters. Next, the self-supervised learning approach is applied to optimize the similarity constraints, which are then used to re-cluster the pixels. This process is repeated until convergence to produce the final classification results. Experimental results on three hyperspectral images demonstrate the proposed method's ability to achieve high accuracy and efficiency in subspace clustering and self-supervised learning.

The Arctic's sea ice is characterized by a complex topography formed by
undulations in the ice surface. When snow accumulates, it creates a distinct
pattern of ridges, which have been extensively studied in the context of
drifting ice floes. In this study, we develop a simplified model that
reproduces the snow topography on undeformed ice by accounting for the
influence of wind on the snow field. The model's parameters are derived from
the statistical properties of the wind field, and its predictions are compared
to actual snow topography on Arctic ice floes. The model's ability to simulate
the snow ridges on undeformed ice demonstrates its effectiveness, and its
results can be used to inform the development of more complex models that
account for the interactions between ice floes and wind-driven drift.

We investigate the impact of a rapidly oscillating magnetic field on the quantum Zeno effect in ultracold atom-molecule scattering. The magnetic field's influence induces a periodic variation in the Zeeman splitting of atomic and molecular energy levels, creating a quantum Zeno effect that can be experimentally verified in a spin-dependent optical lattice. Our findings demonstrate that the effect can be adjusted by controlling the frequency and amplitude of the magnetic field, allowing for the observation of the effect in specific scattering channels. Moreover, we show that the effect can be used to suppress molecule formation in ultracold atom-molecule collisions, paving the way for the study of quantum scattering processes.

We investigate the behavior of a particle system under the influence of non-extensive interactions, which is a common scenario in physical systems. To model this, we utilize the It\^o-Langevin equation, which describes the time-evolution of a particle's phase-space density. Our analysis reveals that the system's density converges to a stable equilibrium state, characterized by a q-Gaussian distribution, where q is determined by the system's parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the rate of convergence is dependent on q and the system's non-extensivity parameter, which is a key finding that can be applied to a broad range of systems governed by non-extensive interactions.

A new type of semimetal is created by manipulating light on a specific surface of a conventional crystal, resulting in a semimetal state that can be controlled with high precision. The surface of this material exhibits a unique property called Weyl nodes, which are critical to its behavior. By adjusting the intensity of the laser, the researchers can control the number of Weyl nodes, making this material highly tunable. The research also reveals that the nodes on the surface of this material have a unique property called inversion-symmetry protected higher-order topology. The study demonstrates that the nodes on the surface of this material have a unique property called zero-dimensional point nodes, which is distinct from the traditional understanding of Weyl nodes. The research provides a new way to create and control topological materials using light, opening up new possibilities for the development of novel photonic devices.

A groundbreaking approach to computing harnesses the power of human intelligence through crowdsourcing, yet its full potential remains unrealized due to the limitations of traditional methods. These include the lack of incentives, which leads to low participation and unreliable results. In response, our research presents Marvel DC, a novel blockchain-based protocol that incentivizes participants and ensures the integrity of the computation process. By utilizing a decentralized network, Marvel DC provides a secure and efficient framework for distributed computing. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this protocol, which has the potential to revolutionize the way distributed computing is conducted.

This research introduces a novel framework for assessing the perceptual quality of compressed video content at a reduced scale. The framework's application extends to evaluating quality in other types of compressed media, such as image and 3D point cloud data. The framework's core is a model that estimates the perceptual quality of compressed video based on the characteristics of the original, uncompressed video. This quality assessment model is trained on a dataset of compressed video samples, which are generated using different compression methods. The framework's utility is demonstrated through its application to the compression of 3D point clouds. The study shows that the framework's quality assessment model performs similarly to a more complex model that estimates quality based on the entire uncompressed video. The framework's reduced reference quality assessment model is then used in a rate control algorithm to achieve a balance between the quality of the compressed video and its file size. The results of the study confirm that the framework's quality assessment model is effective in ensuring that the compressed video meets the required quality standards while keeping the file size under control.

We utilize holography to study the phase map of the temperature-charged chemical potential diagram in QCD. The phase map obtained through our investigation indicates that there are four distinct phases: the hadron gas phase, the chiral liquid phase, the quark gluon plasma phase, and the charged quark matter phase. The chiral liquid and quark gluon plasma phases exhibit second-order end points, while the boundary between the hadron gas and charged quark matter phases shows a unique feature where the hadron gas becomes non-existent. Our findings also suggest that the phase transition between the chiral liquid and quark gluon plasma phases is driven by the influence of the charged chemical potential.

Knee joint anomalies can be challenging to diagnose due to their varied presentation, making early detection crucial for effective treatment.  MRI scans are often the preferred method for assessing structural abnormalities, but they are not always readily available.  To address this issue, we propose a novel approach, known as Slice-Based Self-Supervised Learning (SB-SSL), which leverages self-supervised learning to enhance the effectiveness of anomaly detection from 2D MRI slice scans.
